card.profile: Nine circles to the sun — Ohuokhai (Osuokhai) (Russia, Sakha (Yakutia)). Full sourced 9-field A+ profile in research artifact W10; concise schema stub pending text expansion.
card.image_significance: Nine circles to the sun. A representative image shows ceremonial regalia in a ritual context — imagery should be handled respectfully, not as spectacle — Sakha (Yakutia), Russia.
card.profile_long: The Ohuokhai is a foundational cultural practice of the Sakha people, originating from their history as cattle-breeders and 'sun worshippers' in southern regions. Today, it is most prominently performed during the Yhyakh festival, which celebrates the summer solstice and the rebirth of nature. The dance is a simultaneous performance of movement, song, and poetry, functioning as a communal ritual that connects participants to the natural world. The dance takes place in a large circle, which represents the cycle of life. Participants join hands or link arms, moving in a clockwise direction to mirror the path of the sun, an act believed to allow dancers to capture solar energy for the coming year. The performance is led by a singer who improvises lyrics, which the rest of the circle then repeats, creating a powerful, rhythmic dialogue. This improvisational aspect is considered one of the oldest and richest genres of Sakha folklore. The music is often accompanied by traditional instruments such as the chomus (a jaw harp) and the kyrimpa (a Yakut violin), alongside the unique vocal technique known as Kylyhakh, which involves rapid vocal cord vibration. While the tradition faced periods of stagnation, the 21st century has seen a significant revival of the practice, with competitions held at the national Yhyakh festival to determine the best poetic expression and the largest circle. The dance remains a living tradition, practiced both in the Sakha Republic and by the Sakha diaspora abroad.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance has roots in the period when the Sakha people lived further south as cattle-breeders. It is historically linked to the Yhyakh festival, which celebrates the summer solstice. Following a period of stagnation, the 21st century saw a revival of the tradition.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers form a circle, holding each other by the hand or arm. The movement is performed with the left foot placed forward, following a clockwise direction. The dance is characterized by rhythmic, graceful movements of the body, legs, feet, and arms.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is improvisational, featuring a lead singer who composes poetry on the spot. Key instruments include the chomus (scacciapensieri) and the kyrimpa (Yakut violin). The vocal style includes Kylyhakh, a technique of vocal cord vibration.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed in an 'alas' (a large meadow), often near a 'World Tree' (Aal Luuk Mas). Participants often wear traditional costumes during the Yhyakh festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed during the Yhyakh festival to celebrate the summer solstice, the triumph of life, and the rebirth of nature. It symbolizes the circle of life and the capturing of solar energy.
sections.notable_figures: Sergey Zverev, a folk singer, poet, and composer from the Suntarsky region, is noted for adding new elements to the expressiveness of the movements.
sections.lineage: The dance is a native Sakha tradition, linked to the cult of the sun and fertility.

claims.text: The Ohuokhai (Оhуохай) dance has its roots in the period when the Sakha people lived further south and were cattle-breeders, termed 'sun worshippers'.
Dancers form a circle and dance, arm in arm, hand in hand, with the left foot put forward, while making rhythmical, graceful movements with their bodies, legs, feet and arms.
The Ohuokhai is a simultaneous circle dance and song.
A lead singer improvises the lyrics and the other dancers repeat them.
Kylyhakh is the special singing technique of vocal cord vibration.
The Ohuokhai (Оhуохай) consists of a large circle dance, which symbolizes the circle of life, while singing songs dedicated to the power of nature.
The 21st century saw a revival of Sakha culture, including Yhyakh.
